title: Hautes-Chaumes, A Marcairie Week on the Vosges Crest
subRegion: Parc naturel régional des Ballons des Vosges, Haut-Rhin

bestPeriod.note: Marcairies and fermes-auberges on the hautes-chaumes generally open only from late May to October, when cattle are up on summer pasture.

summary: A week of nights in working marcairies and fermes-auberges on the Vosges high pastures, walking the Route des Crêtes from the Grand Ballon to Lac Blanc.
hook: The Vosges' high pastures, the hautes-chaumes, are one of France's odder landscapes: treeless, wind-combed grassland sitting directly above dense beech and fir forest, grazed all summer by cattle whose milk still goes into real Munster cheese at working farmhouses called marcairies. Several of these farms take overnight guests as fermes-auberges, and this week strings a run of them together along and below the Route des Crêtes, from the Grand Ballon's summit dome to the cliffs above Lac Blanc, with the smell of woodsmoke and warm cheese as the constant.

snapshot.Base(s): Munster valley, with two nights at a hautes-chaumes marcairie (7 nights total)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 65-85 km walking, 2,600-3,200 m cumulative ascent; forest track, open pasture, granite ridge path
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Bâle-Mulhouse-Freiburg (EuroAirport), train to Colmar, then bus or taxi to Munster; a car is genuinely useful for the crest days
snapshot.Who It Suits: Families and moderate walkers who want real farm hospitality alongside their hiking, not a wilderness survival week

itinerary.title: Arrival in Munster
itinerary.morning: Train from Colmar to Munster, the small town that gives its name to the cheese and the valley. Settle into your base and buy provisions for the coming marcairie nights, where meals are often simple and self-catering supplements are welcome.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy orientation walk along the Fecht river through town and out to the edge of the valley's pasture, getting a first look at the hautes-chaumes rising above.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Munster, the town has a proper choice of restaurants, your last for a couple of nights.

itinerary.title: Petit Ballon and first marcairie night
itinerary.morning: Drive to the trailhead near Sondernach and climb through beech forest onto the open chaume of the Petit Ballon (1,267 m), a gentler warm-up before the bigger crest days.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue along the ridge to a working marcairie for the night. The last stretch to most hautes-chaumes farms is an unpaved farm track, generally fine for an ordinary car in dry weather but rutted enough after rain that a higher-clearance vehicle is safer; expect a 10-20 minute walk-in with your overnight bag from the nearest parking turn-out.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the farm: tourte, munster with cumin, a simple tarte aux myrtilles if the season's right. Lights are early here, everyone's up with the cattle.
itinerary.dayStats: 14 km, 700 m ascent. Grade moderate, forest track then open pasture.

itinerary.title: Along the chaume to Le Markstein
itinerary.morning: Walk the ridge path south along the hautes-chaumes toward Le Markstein, through classic high-pasture terrain grazed by Vosgienne cattle, with views opening east toward the Rhine plain and the distant line of the Black Forest.
itinerary.afternoon: Détour to a second ferme-auberge for lunch, a good way to compare the region's cheese-and-charcuterie plates.
itinerary.evening: Return to Munster by car or taxi for a proper shower and a night in a real bed.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 400 m ascent/descent. Grade easy-moderate, open chaume path.

itinerary.title: Grand Ballon and the Route des Crêtes
itinerary.morning: Drive the Route des Crêtes, the WWI-era military road that runs the Vosges skyline, to the base of the Grand Ballon (1,424 m), the range's highest point, topped by a radar dome and a First World War memorial to army engineers.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the short summit loop, then follow the crest road's parallel footpath toward Col Amic, watching the exposed rock for chamois, reintroduced to the Vosges in the 1950s and now established near Hohneck and the Grand Ballon.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km, 350 m ascent/descent. Grade easy, exposed to wind on the summit plateau.

itinerary.title: Hohneck and second marcairie night
itinerary.morning: Drive to the Col de la Schlucht and climb to the Hohneck (1,362 m), one of the most panoramic summits in the range, with the Lac Blanc cirque visible to the north and the Alsace plain spread out east.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend along the ridge to a second marcairie for the night, a different farm from Day 2 to see the variation in the tradition, some run larger dairy herds, others focus more on the auberge side.
itinerary.evening: Farm dinner again; ask about the cheese-making schedule, since some marcairies let guests watch or even help with the morning milking.
itinerary.dayStats: 15 km, 750 m ascent/descent. Grade moderate, ridge path and pasture track.

itinerary.title: Lac Blanc and the Rocher du Hang
itinerary.morning: Walk down from the marcairie toward Lac Blanc, a glacial lake beneath dramatic granite cliffs near Orbey, formed by the same Quaternary glaciation that shaped the whole crest.
itinerary.afternoon: Loop around the lake and up to the Rocher du Hang viewpoint above it, a well-known local paragliding launch, worth watching from below even if you're not flying. Continue to Col du Calvaire and pick up return transport to Munster.
itinerary.evening: Last full evening, dinner in Munster, pack for departure.
itinerary.dayStats: 16 km, 550 m ascent/descent. Grade moderate, forest and lakeside path, some rocky steps near the Rocher du Hang.

itinerary.title: Departure
itinerary.morning: A short farewell walk from Munster into the nearest pasture edge before checkout.
itinerary.afternoon: Bus or taxi to Colmar, train onward to Bâle-Mulhouse-Freiburg.

accommodationStrategy.name: A marcairie/ferme-auberge on the hautes-chaumes
accommodationStrategy.description: The heart of this trip: two separate nights at different working dairy farms that also take overnight guests, chosen for their setting directly on the crest rather than for any particular comfort standard. Rooms are simple, sometimes dormitory-style, and the appeal is entirely the setting and the food, fresh munster, farm charcuterie, and a fire going by evening even in August.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 6-8 weeks ahead for July-August, since many marcairies take only a handful of overnight guests at a time.

accommodationStrategy.name: A guesthouse in Munster
accommodationStrategy.description: Your comfortable middle-of-week base, with a proper shower, a full choice of restaurants, and easy access to the Route des Crêtes trailheads by car. Munster's cheese market and dairy heritage make it a genuinely relevant base rather than just a convenient one.

accommodationStrategy.name: A hotel near Col de la Schlucht
accommodationStrategy.description: Useful if you'd rather stay right on the Route des Crêtes for the Hohneck and Lac Blanc days rather than driving up from the valley each morning; several small hotels sit directly on or near the col.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; French mountain rescue is reached via 112, which routes to the relevant gendarmerie or PGHM unit.
logistics.money: Cards are near-universal in Munster and at most fermes-auberges; carry cash for the smaller, more remote marcairies.

other.label: Isolation, specifically
other.text: Munster has full supermarkets and a pharmacy; the marcairies themselves have no shop at all, phone signal on the open chaume is generally workable but drops in the forested approach sections, and the nearest hospital is in Colmar, roughly 30-40 minutes from Munster.

other.label: Foraging
other.text: Mushroom picking is broadly tolerated in French state and communal forest for personal consumption within informal reasonable limits, but is prohibited or restricted within the park's designated nature reserves, including the Tanet-Gazon du Faing reserve near Hohneck, check signage before picking anywhere near a reserve boundary.

other.label: Fire
other.text: Open fires are prohibited in and near Vosges forest under standing prefectural rules, tightened further during dry summer spells when burn bans are common; the marcairies' own hearths are the fire you get.

other.label: Grand tétras (capercaillie)
other.text: A small, protected population survives in the old-growth stands near Hohneck and the Tanet massif; some paths in this zone carry seasonal or permanent off-trail restrictions to protect breeding birds, stay on marked routes through these sections regardless of season.

other.label: Wildlife
other.text: Chamois are the headline sighting on the rockier crest faces; red deer are present lower in the forest, with the rut running through October; wild boar are common and best given space, especially with dogs.

other.label: Ticks
other.text: Present through the Vosges forest and pasture edges in warmer months; check after every walk.

other.label: Opening hours
other.text: French village shops often close on Monday rather than Sunday, the reverse of the Austrian and German pattern, check the specific day before relying on a small-town boulangerie.

proTips: Book the two marcairie nights first and build driving legs around them, the good ones fill early in July and August precisely because they take so few overnight guests.
Ask each marcairie directly whether you can watch or join the evening milking; it's often offered informally rather than advertised, and it's the most memorable hour of the trip.
Walk the Route des Crêtes on foot for the Grand Ballon-Col Amic stretch rather than only driving it; the parallel footpath gets you off the road and onto genuine pasture within ten minutes.
Time Lac Blanc for a weekday morning, it's one of the most visited spots in the southern Vosges on a fine summer weekend, largely for its paragliding launch and lake views.
Order the munster fermier with cumin seeds specifically, and ask which marcairie made it, much of what's served on the crest comes from the very farm you're eating in.
If chamois-spotting matters to you, glass the rockier north faces near Hohneck in the first two hours after sunrise, before day-hikers are on the ridge.
Carry small cash even at farms that technically take cards, connectivity on the open chaume is patchy enough that terminals sometimes fail.

packingNotes: Sturdy walking shoes for the mix of forest track, pasture and the rockier Rocher du Hang steps.
A proper windproof layer, the open hautes-chaumes are exposed with no tree cover at all.
A change of clothes light enough to carry for the two marcairie nights, since these are walk-in stays.
Cash in small denominations for the more remote farms.
Binoculars for chamois and, in October, listening for the deer rut.
Tick repellent and a tick-removal tool.
A basic first-aid kit, the nearest hospital is 30-40 minutes from Munster.
Sun protection; the chaume has essentially no shade at midday.
A refillable water bottle; farms along the route are generally happy to refill it, but carry enough for the exposed stretches between them.
A camera or phone with a full battery for the Route des Crêtes viewpoints, signal, and therefore charging temptation to check it constantly, is unreliable up there anyway.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A marcairie is fully booked for your preferred date.** Fallback: the park has a genuine network of these farms along the crest; ask the Munster tourist office for current availability.
**Rain turns the farm access track to mud.** Fallback: park at the lower turn-out and walk the last stretch in; call ahead so the farm knows.
**Wind or storm makes the exposed Grand Ballon-Hohneck stretch unpleasant.** Fallback: drop into the forest paths just below the crest line, which run roughly parallel and stay sheltered.

**A summer burn ban is in effect and you're relying on an open fire for warmth.** Fallback: the marcairies' indoor hearths are unaffected; just don't expect or ask for anything outdoors during a dry-spell restriction.

**Lac Blanc is unpleasantly crowded on a summer Saturday.** Fallback: shift that leg to Sunday morning instead, or walk the quieter approach from Col du Calvaire rather than the main Orbey-side car park route.
